metadata.title: marco-david/ainfinity-lean (Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: The tikz lattice diagram of the B_i complexes with g and h arrows is a figure; it was not extracted (the prose before and after it is).
Remark 3 of Section 6.4.4 is an empty environment; no node. Sections 6.1, 6.5 and 6.6 are empty headings.
The [SF_n] axioms are bold-labelled prose conditions a braiding functor must satisfy; typed definition rather than assumption.
Macros \Ainf, \C, \CMat, \KLRW are not expanded in the prepared source; some definitions have duplicated or missing words (DP33 repeats a phrase, DP23 has a gap where a Lean term was).

metadata.extraction_comment: Lean blueprint: proofs are mostly one-line pointers to formal code; the KLRW chapter is informal construction prose.

nodes.name: Grading type
nodes.statement: A grading type is an abelian group $\beta$ together with group homomorphisms \[ \operatorname{shift} : \mathbb{Z} \to \beta, \qquad \operatorname{sign} : \beta \to \{\pm 1\}, \] such that $\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{shift}(1)) = -1$; that is, the differential, which has degree $\operatorname{shift}(1)$, is odd. For a degree $d \in \beta$ we write $(-1)^d := \operatorname{sign}(d)$ for its Koszul sign.
nodes.statement_short: An abelian group of degrees with an integer shift map and a Koszul sign character, where shift(1) is odd.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType

nodes.name: Sign of an integer shift
nodes.statement: For every integer $n$ one has $(-1)^{\operatorname{shift}(n)} = (-1)^n$.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.sign_shift

nodes.name: Proof of sign of an integer shift
nodes.statement: Since $\operatorname{shift}(n) = n \cdot \operatorname{shift}(1)$ and $\operatorname{sign}$ is a homomorphism, $(-1)^{\operatorname{shift}(n)} = \operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{shift}(1))^n = (-1)^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Write shift(n) = n·shift(1) and use that sign is a homomorphism.

nodes.name: Standard gradings
nodes.statement: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ form a grading type with $\operatorname{shift}$ the identity and $\operatorname{sign}(n) = (-1)^n$. The parities $\mathbb{Z}/2$ form a grading type with $\operatorname{shift}$ the reduction modulo $2$ and $\operatorname{sign}(p) = (-1)^p$.
nodes.statement_short: Integers and parities as grading types with the evident shift and sign.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType.standard

nodes.name: Product gradings
nodes.statement: Let $\beta$ be a grading type and $\gamma$ an abelian group. The product $\beta \times \gamma$ is a grading type with $\operatorname{shift}(n) = (\operatorname{shift}(n), 0)$ in two ways: either the sign is read off the first factor alone, $\operatorname{sign}(b,c) = (-1)^b$, or, when $\gamma$ is a grading type as well, the sign is the total sign $\operatorname{sign}(b,c) = (-1)^b\,(-1)^c$. Neither choice is canonical, so both are constructions to be activated locally rather than instances.
nodes.statement_short: Product of a grading type with an abelian group, with sign from the first factor or the total sign.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType.prod

nodes.name: Graded linear map
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a semiring and let $M, N$ be $\beta$-indexed families of $R$-modules. A graded $R$-linear map $f : M \to N$ of degree $d \in \beta$ consists of an $R$-linear map $f_{i,j} : M(i) \to N(j)$ for every pair of degrees with $i + d = j$. Graded linear maps of degree $d$ form an $R$-module under componentwise operations.
nodes.statement_short: A degree-d family of linear maps M(i) → N(i+d); these form an R-module.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearMap

nodes.name: Composition of graded linear maps
nodes.statement: The composite of graded linear maps of degrees $d$ and $e$ is a graded linear map of degree $d + e$, whose component from degree $i$ factors through degree $i + d$. The identity is a graded linear map of degree $0$. Composition is associative and unital.
conclusions: The composite of graded linear maps of degrees $d$ and $e$ is a graded linear map of degree $d + e$, whose component from degree $i$ factors through degree $i + d$.
The identity is a graded linear map of degree $0$.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearMap.comp

nodes.name: Proof of composition of graded linear maps
nodes.statement: Componentwise, this is associativity and unitality of composition of linear maps, once every component of a composite is seen to factor through any middle degree.
nodes.statement_short: Componentwise reduction to associativity and unitality of linear map composition.

nodes.name: Graded multilinear map
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a semiring, let $(M_j)_{j \in \iota}$ be a finite family of $\beta$-indexed families of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be a $\beta$-indexed family of $R$-modules. A graded $R$-multilinear map of degree $d \in \beta$ consists, for every choice of input degrees $(d_j)_{j \in \iota}$ and every output degree $i$ with $\sum_j d_j + d = i$, of an $R$-multilinear map \[ \prod_j M_j(d_j) \to N(i). \] Graded multilinear maps of degree $d$ form an $R$-module under componentwise operations.
nodes.statement_short: A degree-d family of multilinear maps from products of graded pieces into N(sum of degrees + d).
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedMultilinearMap

nodes.name: Graded linear quiver
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring $R$, a graded $R$-linear quiver on an object type $\mathrm{Obj}$ assigns to each pair of objects $(X,Y)$ and each degree $i \in \beta$ an $R$-module $\Hom(X,Y)_i$ of morphisms of degree $i$ from $X$ to $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Assigns to each pair of objects and each degree a module of morphisms of that degree.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearQuiver

nodes.name: Operation target degree
nodes.statement: Given input degrees $(d_0,\dots,d_{n-1})$ in a grading type $\beta$, the output degree of the $n$-ary operation is \[ \sum_i d_i + \operatorname{shift}(2-n), \] where the final summand is the image of the integer $2-n$ under the shift homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \beta$.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.operationTargetDeg

nodes.name: Stasheff target degree
nodes.statement: The common degree of the arity-$n$ Stasheff relation is \[ \sum_i d_i + \operatorname{shift}(3-n) \] in the grading type.
nodes.definiendum: common degree of the arity-$n$ Stasheff relation
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.stasheffTargetDeg

nodes.name: Composable morphism type
nodes.statement: For a string of objects $X_0,\dots,X_n$, an index $i < n$ and a degree $b$, this is the hom-module $\Hom(X_i, X_{i+1})_b$ of the $i$-th morphism in that composable string, in degree $b$.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearQuiver.ComposableHomType

nodes.name: A-infinity composition
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-composition on a graded quiver $\Hom$ assigns to every positive arity $n$ and every string of objects $X_0,\dots,X_n$ a graded multilinear map \[ m_n : \Hom(X_0,X_1) \times \cdots \times \Hom(X_{n-1},X_n) \to \Hom(X_0,X_n) \] of degree $\operatorname{shift}(2-n)$. Thus for input degrees $(d_0,\dots,d_{n-1})$ its component lands in any degree equal to the operation target degree.
nodes.statement_short: Graded multilinear operations m_n of degree shift(2-n) on every composable string of objects.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.AInfinityComposition

nodes.name: Indexed Stasheff term
nodes.statement: Fix an \Ainf{}-composition $m$. For $r + s + t = n$ with $s \geq 1$, is the term obtained by first applying the inner $s$-ary operation in positions $r,\dots,r+s-1$ and then applying the outer $(r+1+t)$-ary operation to the collapsed string. It lies in $\Hom(X_0,X_n)$ in any degree equal to the Stasheff target degree.
nodes.statement_short: The composite of an inner s-ary operation in positions r..r+s-1 followed by the outer (r+1+t)-ary operation.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.indexedStasheffTerm

nodes.name: Stasheff sign
nodes.statement: The sign $\pm 1$ attached to $(r,s,t)$ is \[ \prod_{k=r+s}^{n-1} (-1)^{\|a_k\|}, \qquad \|a_k\| := |a_k| - \operatorname{shift}(1), \] the product of the Koszul signs of the reduced degrees of the $t$ trailing inputs. Since the sign character is a homomorphism, this equals $(-1)^{|a_{r+s}| + \cdots + |a_{n-1}| - \operatorname{shift}(t)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Product of Koszul signs of the reduced degrees of the t trailing inputs.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.stasheffSign

nodes.name: Indexed Stasheff sum
nodes.statement: The arity-$n$ Stasheff sum is the signed sum of all valid composites of an inner operation followed by an outer operation, that is, of the Stasheff terms indexed by $0 \leq r \leq n$ and $1 \leq s \leq n - r$, with $t = n - r - s$. It lies in $\Hom(X_0,X_n)$ in any degree equal to the Stasheff target degree.
nodes.statement_short: Signed sum of all Stasheff terms over valid (r,s,t).
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.indexedStasheffSum

nodes.name: Indexed Stasheff identities
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-composition satisfies the Stasheff identities if every indexed Stasheff sum vanishes, for every positive arity, string of objects, choice of input degrees and composable inputs.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.indexedSatisfiesStasheff

nodes.name: A-infinity precategory
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-precategory over $R$ with object type $\mathrm{Obj}$ consists of a graded $R$-linear quiver \[ \Hom : \mathrm{Obj} \to \mathrm{Obj} \to \grMod_R^\beta \] together with an \Ainf{}-composition, that is, operations \[ m_n : \Hom(X_0, X_1) \otimes \dots \otimes \Hom(X_{n-1}, X_n) \to \Hom(X_0, X_n) \] of degree $\operatorname{shift}(2-n)$ for every positive arity $n>0$. No relations are imposed on these composition maps.
nodes.statement_short: A graded linear quiver with operations m_n of degree shift(2-n), no relations imposed.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.AInfinityCategoryStruct

nodes.name: Chain
nodes.statement: A chain in an \Ainf{}-precategory consists of a positive length $n$, a string of $n+1$ objects, and a degree assigned to each of the $n$ composable morphism slots.
nodes.label: AInfinityCategoryTheory.AInfinityPreCategory.Chain

nodes.name: Chain source
nodes.statement: The source of a chain is its initial object.
nodes.label: AInfinityCategoryTheory.AInfinityPreCategory.Chain.source

nodes.name: Chain target
nodes.statement: The target of a chain is its final object.
nodes.label: AInfinityCategoryTheory.AInfinityPreCategory.Chain.target

nodes.name: Chain link type
nodes.statement: For a chain and an index $i$, \texttt{Chain.link} is the module of the $i$-th composable morphism in that chain.
nodes.label: AInfinityCategoryTheory.AInfinityPreCategory.Chain.link

nodes.name: Chain operation target
nodes.statement: For a chain, this is the graded hom-module that receives the corresponding multilinear operation.
nodes.label: AInfinityCategoryTheory.AInfinityPreCategory.Chain.operationTarget

nodes.name: A-infinity category
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-category is an \Ainf{}-precategory together with a proof that its operations satisfy the Stasheff identities.
differentia: its operations satisfy the Stasheff identities
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.AInfinityCategory

nodes.name: Stasheff sum vanishes in an A-infinity category
nodes.statement: For an \Ainf{}-category, every Stasheff sum computed from the structure maps is equal to zero.
conclusions: every Stasheff sum computed from the structure maps is equal to zero
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.AInfinityCategory.indexedStasheffSum_eq_zero

nodes.name: Proof that the Stasheff sum vanishes in an A-infinity category
nodes.statement: This is the Stasheff identity that is part of the data of an \Ainf{}-category.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the Stasheff identity included in the data.

nodes.name: A-infinity algebra structure
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a graded $R$-module. An \Ainf{}-algebra structure on $A$ consists of multilinear operations \[ m_n : A(d_0) \otimes \cdots \otimes A(d_{n-1}) \to A\!\left(\sum_i d_i + \operatorname{shift}(2 - n)\right) \] for every positive arity $n$ and every choice of input degrees.
nodes.statement_short: Multilinear operations m_n of degree shift(2-n) on a graded module for every positive arity.
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgStruct

nodes.name: Algebra to precategory
nodes.statement: Any \Ainf{}-algebra structure determines a one-object \Ainf{}-precategory, with object type and constant hom-module equal to the underlying graded module.
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgStruct.toPreCategory

nodes.name: Algebra Stasheff sum
nodes.statement: The Stasheff sum of an \Ainf{}-algebra is the Stasheff sum of its associated one-object \Ainf{}-precategory.
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgStruct.stasheffSum

nodes.name: Algebra Stasheff property
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-algebra structure satisfies the Stasheff identities when every one of its Stasheff sums is zero.
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgStruct.satisfiesStasheff

nodes.name: A-infinity algebra
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-algebra is an \Ainf{}-algebra structure together with a proof of the Stasheff identities.
differentia: together with a proof of the Stasheff identities
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgebra

nodes.name: Stasheff sum vanishes in an A-infinity algebra
nodes.statement: For an \Ainf{}-algebra, every algebraic Stasheff sum is equal to zero.
conclusions: every algebraic Stasheff sum is equal to zero
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgebra.stasheff_eq_zero

nodes.name: A-infinity algebra to precategory
nodes.statement: An \Ainf{}-algebra canonically determines a one-object \Ainf{}-precategory.
nodes.label: AInfinityAlgebraTheory.AInfinityAlgebra.toPreCategory

nodes.name: Computable additive completion
nodes.statement: Let $\C$ be a preadditive category. Then the \emph{computable additive completion} of $\C$, denoted $\operatorname{CMat}(\C)$, has \begin{itemize} \item as objects, lists of elements in $\C$. \item as morphisms, dependent matrices of morphisms in $\C$. Specifically, if $(A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_n), (B_0, B_1, \ldots, B_m) \in \Ob\big(\Mat(\C)\big)$, then \begin{multline*} \Hom\big((A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_n), (B_0, B_1, \ldots, B_m)\big) \\ = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} a_{00} & \cdots & a_{0,n-1} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{m-1,0} & \cdots & a_{m-1,n-1} \end{bmatrix} : a_{ij} \in \Hom(A_j, B_i) \right\} \end{multline*} where $0 \le i \le m-1$ and $0 \le j \le n-1$. \item composition is defined by matrix multiplication \item identities are given by the identity matrix $$ (\idf_{(A_0, \ldots, A_m)})_{i, j} = \begin{cases} \idf_{A_i} & \text{reinterpreted as an element of }\Hom(A_i, A_j) \text{ by casting along the equality if }i = j \\ 0 & \text{ if }i\ne j \end{cases}$$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Objects are lists of objects of C, morphisms are dependent matrices, composition by matrix multiplication.

nodes.name: Fully faithful functor into the computable additive completion
nodes.statement: There is a fully faithful functor $G: \C \Rightarrow \CMat(\C)$.
conclusions: There is a fully faithful functor $G: \C \Rightarrow \CMat(\C)$.

nodes.name: Computable additive completion is equivalent to the additive completion
nodes.statement: There is a fully faithful embedding functor $F: \CMat(\C) \Rightarrow \Mat (\C)$. It is (nonconstructively) essentially surjective, so $F$ is an equivalence of categories.
conclusions: There is a fully faithful embedding functor $F: \CMat(\C) \Rightarrow \Mat (\C)$.

nodes.name: Computable biproduct
nodes.statement: Given $A = (A_0, \ldots, A_n), B=(B_0, \ldots, B_n)\in \CMat(\C)$, the \emph{computable biproduct} of $A$ and $B$ is defined by $A\boxplus_k B = (A_0, \ldots, A_n, B_0, \ldots, B_m)$

nodes.name: Index type
nodes.statement: For any $Z\in \CMat (\C)$, the \emph{index type}, denoted $\iota_Z$, is the type $\{ 0, \ldots, (\len(Z)-1)\}$, and the indexing function, $X_2: \iota_Z\to \C$, is defined by $X_Z(i) = Z_i$.

nodes.name: Positioning and strand space
nodes.statement: Let $n\in \N$. A \emph{positioning} of $1$ black strand with $n$ red strands is an element of $\{0, \ldots, n+1\}$. Given positionings of $X$ and $Y$, the strand set $StrandSpace_{X, Y} = \N$, representing the number of dots. (Note here that $\StrandSpace_{X, Y}$ does not depend on $X$ or $Y$, but with more black strands it might).
nodes.statement_short: A position of one black strand among n red strands; the strand space of a pair is N (number of dots).

nodes.name: Composition in the strand space
nodes.statement: If $X, Y, Z$ are positionings of $1$ black strand and $n$ red strands and $a\in \StrandSpace_{X, Y}$, $b\in \StrandSpace_{Y, Z}$, then their composition is given by \begin{align*} b\circ a &= a + b + \frac{|X-Y| + |Y-Z| - |X-Z|}{2} \\ &= a + b + \max (x, y) + \max (y, z) - \max (x, z) - y \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Dot counts add, plus a correction term from the crossing geometry of the three positionings.

nodes.name: KLRW category
nodes.statement: Fix a commutative ring $R$. The $\KLRW$ category of $1$ black strand and $n$ red strands, denoted $\KLRW$ category of $1$ black strand and $n$ red strands, denoted $\KLRW^R_n$, is given by \begin{itemize} \item $\Ob(\KLRW^R_n)$ is the set of positionings of $1$ black strand with $n$ red strands \item $\Hom(X, Y)$ is the free $R$-module generated by $\StrandSpace_{X, Y}$. \end{itemize} Composition in $\KLRW^R_n$ is defined by extending the composition of elements of the strand space linearly. Since each $\Hom(X, Y)$ is an $R$-module and composition is $R$-linear, $\KLRW^R_n$ is $R$-linear and thus preadditive.
nodes.statement_short: Objects are positionings, homs are free R-modules on the strand space, composition extended linearly.

nodes.name: Bounded cochain complex
nodes.statement: Let $\C$ be a preadditive category with a zero object. Then a bounded cochain complex of $\C$ is a ($\Z$-graded) cochain complex $A^\bullet$ of $\C$ equipped with a finite set $S$ called the support, satisfying $\forall i\in \Z, i\in S \Leftrightarrow A^i\not\cong 0$. Note that $S$ is uniquely determined by $A^\bullet$, though included for computability.
differentia: equipped with a finite set $S$ called the support

nodes.name: Category of bounded cochain complexes
nodes.statement: Let $\BK(\C)$ denote the set of bounded cochain complexes in $\C$. THen there is a function $F:\BK(\C)\to K^\bullet(\C)$ which forgets the finiteness. Then we equip $\BK(\C)$ with the induced category structure of $F$ which makes $F$ into a fully faithful functor $F:\BK(\C) \to K^\bullet (\C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded cochain complexes with the category structure induced by the forgetful map to K(C).

nodes.name: Braiding functor data
nodes.statement: Let $R, S, T \in \mathcal{KLRW}$. The data of a braiding functor is given by the following functions: $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_0 &\colon & \mathcal{KLRW} &\to K^\bullet \\ \beta_1 &\colon & \operatorname{Hom}(R,S) &\to \operatorname{Hom}(\beta_0(R), \beta_0(S)) \\ \beta_2 &\colon & \operatorname{Hom}(R,S) \times \operatorname{Hom}(S,T) &\to \operatorname{Hom}(\beta_0(R), \beta_0(T)) \end{aligned} $$ In addition to these functions, there must also be proofs that they satisfy $A_\infty$ relations.
nodes.statement_short: A braiding functor is given by maps β0 on objects, β1 on morphisms and β2 on pairs, plus proofs of the A∞ relations.

nodes.name: beta_0.add
nodes.statement: We define: $$\widehat{\beta}_0 \colon \operatorname{Add}(\mathcal{KLRW}) \to K^\bullet$$ by setting: $$\widehat{\beta}_0\left(\bigoplus_i S_i\right) = \bigoplus_i \beta_0(S_i)$$
nodes.statement_short: Extend β0 to Add(KLRW) by direct sums.

nodes.name: beta_1.add
nodes.statement: For $\beta_1$, let $\bigoplus_i A_i$ and $\bigoplus_j B_j$ be objects in $\operatorname{Add}(\mathcal{KLRW})$. Let $f \in \operatorname{Hom}\left(\bigoplus_i A_i, \bigoplus_j B_j\right)$. For each pair $k, l$, we project $f$ to its component $f_{k,l} \in \operatorname{Hom}(A_k, B_l)$. We now create $g_{k,l} \in \operatorname{Hom}\left(\widehat{\beta}_0\left(\bigoplus_i A_i\right), \widehat{\beta}_0\left(\bigoplus_j B_j\right)\right)$ by extending this morphism. Formally, $g_{k,l}$ is constructed by composing the canonical projection, the mapped component, and the canonical injection: $$\widehat{\beta}_0\left(\bigoplus_i A_i\right) \twoheadrightarrow {\beta}_0(A_k) \xrightarrow{\beta_1(f_{k,l})} {\beta}_0(B_l) \hookrightarrow \widehat{\beta}_0\left(\bigoplus_j B_j\right)$$
nodes.statement_short: Extend β1 to matrices: each component f_{k,l} is mapped by β1 and conjugated by the canonical projection and injection.

nodes.name: beta_2.add
nodes.statement: For $\beta_2$, we construct the extension $\widehat{\beta}_2$ analogously.

nodes.name: beta_0.full
nodes.statement: We now define the action of $\beta$ on a chain complex, i.e. the function \begin{equation*} \beta_0.full: K^\bullet AddKLRW \rightarrow K^\bullet AddKLRW. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Idea of the beta_0.full construction
nodes.statement: The idea is as follows. The definition takes use of chain complexes of block matrices, i.e. elements in $K^\bullet AddAddKLRW$. After constructing an element there, we project into $K^\bullet AddKLRW$.

nodes.name: Cochain complex A^*
nodes.statement: Let $A^*$ denote the following cochain complex \[ \cdots \to 0 \to A^{\ell} \xrightarrow{d^{\ell}} A^{\ell+1} \xrightarrow{d^{\ell+1}} \cdots \xrightarrow{d^{r-1}} A^{r} \to 0 \to \cdots \]

nodes.name: Cochain complexes B_i^*
nodes.statement: For any $A^i$, consider $B_i ^*:=\beta_0.add(A^i)$ to be the following cochain complex: \[ \cdots \to 0 \to B^{\ell_i}_{i} \xrightarrow{f_i^{\ell_i}} B^{\ell_i+1}_{i} \xrightarrow{f_i^{\ell_i+1}} \cdots \xrightarrow{f_i^{r_i-1}} B^{r_i}_{i} \to 0 \to \cdots \] where the left and right bounds are $l_i$ and $r_i$.

nodes.name: Chain maps g_i
nodes.statement: For any $d^i:A^i -> A^{i+1}$, we get $g_i:=\beta_1.add(d^i): B_i ^* \to B_{i+1}^*$.

nodes.name: Correction maps h_i
nodes.statement: For any two $d^i:A^i -> A^{i+1}, d^{i+1}:A^{i+1} -> A^{i+2}$, we get $h_i:=\beta_2.add(d^i,d^{i+1}): B_i ^* \to B_{i+2}^*[1]$.

nodes.name: Total complex along diagonals
nodes.statement: The cochain complex which we want, is then obtained by taking direct sums along the diagonals.

nodes.name: Diagonal sum is a cochain complex
nodes.statement: The $A_\infty$-relations ensure that the resulting object is a cochain complex.
conclusions: the resulting object is a cochain complex

nodes.name: Objects of the block-matrix complex
nodes.statement: Construct first the following object in $K^\bullet AddAddKLRW$. The objects of the chain complex will be $\mathbb{Z}$-indexed, where each entry is a list of elements in $AddKLRW$. For an index $k$, the element will be the list $\overline{B}^k:=[B_l ^k, B_{l+1}^{k-1},\dots ,B_r ^{k-r+l}]$.

nodes.name: Bounds of the block-matrix complex
nodes.statement: The bounds are as follows. If $L_i$ and $R_i$ is the lower and upper bound of $B_i$, then our lower bound will be $min(L_i-i)$ and the upper bound will be $max(R_i-i)$. The entry will be the $0$-list outside the bounds.

nodes.name: Differential of the block-matrix complex
nodes.statement: The morphisms will be block matrices, where each entry in the matrix is a morphism between entries in the lists (and thus matrices). For $k$ in these bounds, the morphism $\overline{B}^k\to \overline{B}^{k+1}$ is given by the lower-triangular matrix of the form \[ \begin{pmatrix} f & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ g & f & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ h & g & f & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & h & g & f & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & f \end{pmatrix} \] The $f$'s are the differentials of $B^*_i$, the $g$'s are the chain maps, and the $h$'s are the correction maps. Indices are omitted, but should be possible to infer.
nodes.statement_short: The differential is a lower-triangular block matrix with differentials f on the diagonal, chain maps g and corrections h below.

nodes.name: Why the block matrix is a differential
nodes.statement: For this to be a differential, it would need to square to 0. This gives rise to the following equations: \begin{align} f^2 &= 0 \\ fg + gf &= 0 \\ fh + g^2 + hf &= 0 \\ gh + hg &= 0 \\ h^2 &= 0 \end{align} These can be interpreted as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Equation \ref{eq:f-squared} ensures $f$ is a differential. \item Equation \ref{eq:anticomm-fg} ensures $g$ is a chain map: it is $SF_1$ applied to the input differential $d^i$. \item Equation \ref{eq:cross-term}, \ref{eq:anticomm-gh} and \ref{eq:h-squared} are the equations corresponding to $SF_2$, $SF_3$ and $SF_4$ respectively, after simplifying with the source differential relation $d^{i+1}d^i=0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square of the block matrix into five equations and match each with f^2=0 or an SF axiom.

nodes.name: Anticommutation of f and g
nodes.statement: fg + gf &= 0

nodes.name: Cross term equation
nodes.statement: fh + g^2 + hf &= 0
nodes.label: eq:cross-term

nodes.name: Anticommutation of g and h
nodes.statement: gh + hg &= 0

nodes.name: Squaring the block matrix gives five equations.
nodes.statement: For this to be a differential, it would need to square to 0. This gives rise to the following equations: \begin{align} f^2 &= 0 \\ fg + gf &= 0 \\ fh + g^2 + hf &= 0 \\ gh + hg &= 0 \\ h^2 &= 0 \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Squaring the block matrix gives five equations.

nodes.name: Match each equation with a relation.
nodes.statement: These can be interpreted as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Equation \ref{eq:f-squared} ensures $f$ is a differential. \item Equation \ref{eq:anticomm-fg} ensures $g$ is a chain map: it is $SF_1$ applied to the input differential $d^i$. \item Equation \ref{eq:cross-term}, \ref{eq:anticomm-gh} and \ref{eq:h-squared} are the equations corresponding to $SF_2$, $SF_3$ and $SF_4$ respectively, after simplifying with the source differential relation $d^{i+1}d^i=0$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Why the A-infinity functor axioms reduce to a finite list
nodes.statement: The category $K^\bullet(\operatorname{Add}(KLRW))$ only has differential $\mu_1$ and composition $\mu_2$. Similarly, the braiding functor has no components higher than $\beta_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Only μ1, μ2 and β1, β2 are nonzero, so higher axioms vanish.

nodes.name: Finite list of SF axioms
nodes.statement: Therefore the general $[\text{SF}_n]$ axioms for A-$\infty$ functors reduce to a finite list.
conclusions: the general $[\text{SF}_n]$ axioms for A-$\infty$ functors reduce to a finite list

nodes.name: [SF_1] axiom
nodes.statement: \textbf{[SF\textsubscript{1}].} For all $f \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(A, B)$, $$ \delta_{\beta_0(B)} \circ \beta_1(f) + \beta_1(f) \circ \delta_{\beta_0(A)} = 0. $$ That is, $\beta_1(f)$ is a chain map from $\beta_0(A)$ to $\beta_0(B)$.
nodes.statement_short: β1(f) commutes (up to sign) with the differentials, i.e. is a chain map.

nodes.name: SF_1 is automatic
nodes.statement: This axiom is automatic from the typing of $\beta_1$: its codomain consists of morphisms of cochain complexes, which by definition commute with differentials.

nodes.name: [SF_2] axiom
nodes.statement: \textbf{[SF\textsubscript{2}].} For all composable $f \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(A, B)$ and $g \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(B, C)$, $$ \beta_1(g \circ f) - \beta_1(g) \circ \beta_1(f) = \delta_{\beta_0(C)} \circ \beta_2(f, g) + \beta_2(f, g) \circ \delta_{\beta_0(A)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: β1 fails to be multiplicative by a homotopy given by β2.

nodes.name: [SF_3] axiom
nodes.statement: \textbf{[SF\textsubscript{3}].} For all $f \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(A, B)$, $g \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(B, C)$, and $h \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(C, D)$, $$ \beta_2(f, h \circ g) - \beta_2(g \circ f, h) = \beta_1(h) \circ \beta_2(f, g) - \beta_2(g, h)\circ \beta_1(f). $$
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility of β2 with composition, corrected by β1∘β2 terms.

nodes.name: [SF_4] axiom
nodes.statement: \textbf{[SF\textsubscript{4}].} For all (composable) $f \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(A, B)$, $g \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(B, C)$, $h \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(C, D)$, and $k \in \Hom_{\KLRW}(D, E)$, $$ \beta_2(h, k) \circ \beta_2(f, g)= 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: Composites of two β2 maps vanish.

nodes.name: Vanishing of higher SF axioms
nodes.statement: Since $\beta_2$ produces degree $-1$ maps, their composition has degree $-2$. This axiom says this composition vanishes. For $n \geq 5$, all $[\mathrm{SF}_n]$ axioms are identically zero because every term involves either $\beta_k$ with $k \geq 3$ or $\mu_k$ with $k \geq 3$, both of which are zero.
